# Constraints and Duality {#sec-constraints}

Most real problems come with conditions that must hold exactly: a budget that cannot be
exceeded, weights that must sum to one, a physical quantity that cannot be negative.
@sec-least-squares handled the simplest such condition, a box, by clipping. This chapter
handles general constraints. The central fact is that at a constrained optimum the
gradient of the objective usually does *not* vanish: the boundary is pushing back, and
the force it pushes with, the **Lagrange multiplier**, turns out to be one of the most
useful numbers in optimization. It gives the optimality conditions (KKT), a second,
"dual" problem whose answer bounds and certifies the first, a price for every constraint,
and two very different algorithms: the barrier method, which keeps the iterates strictly
inside the feasible region, and ADMM, which splits a problem into pieces that are each
easy. The chapter ends with problems where the unknown is a whole function.

## The problem

::: {.callout-note title="Definition — Constrained optimization problem"}
$$
\min_{x \in \mathbb{R}^n} f(x)
\quad \text{subject to} \quad
g_i(x) \le 0, \;\; i = 1, \dots, m, \qquad
Cx = d .
$$
The set of points satisfying all constraints is the **feasible set**. An inequality is
**active** at $x$ if $g_i(x) = 0$ and **inactive** if $g_i(x) < 0$.
:::

The problem is **convex** when $f$ and every $g_i$ are convex and the equality
constraints are linear; the feasible set is then convex, and @sec-geometry's guarantee
applies: every local minimum is global.

## Equality constraints and Lagrange multipliers

Start with a single equality constraint, a curve $\{x : c(x) = 0\}$ in the plane. Walk
along the curve. At a constrained minimum, $f$ cannot decrease in either direction along
it, so the directional derivative of $f$ along the curve's tangent is zero: $\nabla f$
is perpendicular to the curve. But $\nabla c$ is also perpendicular to the curve (it is
perpendicular to its own level set, by @sec-geometry). Two vectors perpendicular to the
same line are parallel, so
$$
\nabla f(x^\star) + \nu\, \nabla c(x^\star) = 0 \quad \text{for some number } \nu .
$$
The **Lagrangian** $\mathcal{L}(x, \nu) = f(x) + \nu\, c(x)$ packages this: its gradient
in $x$ is the condition above, its gradient in $\nu$ is the constraint itself. A
constrained problem in $x$ becomes the search for a stationary point of $\mathcal{L}$ in
$(x, \nu)$.

The multiplier has a meaning beyond bookkeeping. If the constraint is relaxed to
$c(x) = \epsilon$, the optimal value changes at rate $-\nu$:
$$
\frac{d f^\star}{d\epsilon} = -\nu .
$$
The multiplier is the **price** of the constraint, the marginal value of loosening it.

### Equality-constrained quadratic programs

For a quadratic objective $\tfrac12 x^\top Q x + q^\top x$ with linear constraints
$Cx = d$, the stationarity conditions are linear, and the whole problem reduces to one
linear system, the **KKT system**:
$$
\begin{bmatrix} Q & C^\top \\ C & 0 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} x \\ \nu \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix} -q \\ d \end{bmatrix} .
$$
Least squares with linear constraints is a special case. Forcing the slope and intercept
of a fitted line to sum to one:

```{python}
#| label: kkt-qp
import numpy as np

from optimlab.linalg import equality_constrained_least_squares, least_squares
from optimlab.viz import markdown_table

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
t = np.linspace(0, 10, 40)
y = 2.0 * t + 1.0 + rng.normal(scale=2.0, size=t.size)
A = np.column_stack([t, np.ones_like(t)])
C, d = np.array([[1.0, 1.0]]), np.array([1.0])  # slope + intercept = 1

free = least_squares(A, y).x
constrained = equality_constrained_least_squares(A, y, C, d)
markdown_table(
    ["fit", "slope", "intercept", "slope + intercept"],
    [("unconstrained", f"{free[0]:.3f}", f"{free[1]:.3f}", f"{free.sum():.3f}"),
     ("constrained", f"{constrained[0]:.3f}", f"{constrained[1]:.3f}",
      f"{constrained.sum():.3f}")],
)
```

The constraint holds exactly, and the fit gives up as little squared error as it can to
satisfy it. @sec-applications uses the same KKT system to compute an efficient
investment portfolio.

## Inequality constraints: the KKT conditions

An inequality $g_i(x) \le 0$ behaves like an equality when it is active and like nothing
at all when it is not. It can also push in only one direction: it can stop $x$ from
leaving the feasible set, never pull it outward. These two facts become the last two of
the four conditions below.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition — Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions"}
With Lagrangian $\mathcal{L}(x, \lambda, \nu) = f(x) + \sum_i \lambda_i g_i(x) +
\nu^\top (Cx - d)$, a point $x^\star$ with multipliers $\lambda^\star, \nu^\star$
satisfies the KKT conditions if

1. **Stationarity**: $\nabla f(x^\star) + \sum_i \lambda_i^\star \nabla g_i(x^\star) +
   C^\top \nu^\star = 0$;
2. **Primal feasibility**: $g_i(x^\star) \le 0$ and $Cx^\star = d$;
3. **Dual feasibility**: $\lambda_i^\star \ge 0$;
4. **Complementary slackness**: $\lambda_i^\star\, g_i(x^\star) = 0$ for every $i$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Theorem — KKT conditions are necessary, and for convex problems sufficient"}
Under a mild regularity assumption on the constraints (a *constraint qualification*;
for convex problems, Slater's condition, the existence of a strictly feasible point,
suffices), every local minimum satisfies the KKT conditions for some multipliers. For a
convex problem, any point satisfying them is a global minimum [@boyd2004convex, §5.5].
:::

Read together, the conditions say: at the optimum, the direction that would improve $f$
fastest, $-\nabla f(x^\star)$, is exactly balanced by the outward normals of the active
constraints, each scaled by a nonnegative multiplier. If it were not balanced, some
feasible direction would still improve $f$. Complementary slackness says an inactive
constraint has a zero multiplier and plays no part in the balance; a constraint that is
not binding has no price. These conditions generalize $\nabla f(x^\star) = 0$, which is
what they reduce to when no constraint is active.

## Duality

The multipliers do more than describe the optimum. Each choice of them defines a lower
bound on the optimal value.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition — Lagrange dual problem"}
The **dual function** is $q(\lambda, \nu) = \inf_x \mathcal{L}(x, \lambda, \nu)$, and the
**dual problem** is
$$
\max_{\lambda \ge 0,\, \nu} \; q(\lambda, \nu) .
$$
:::

**Weak duality** takes one line: for any feasible $x$ and any $\lambda \ge 0$, the added
terms $\lambda_i g_i(x)$ are $\le 0$ and $\nu^\top(Cx - d) = 0$, so
$q(\lambda, \nu) \le \mathcal{L}(x, \lambda, \nu) \le f(x)$. Every dual-feasible point
bounds the primal optimum from below, whether or not the problem is convex. The
difference between a primal objective value and a dual one is the **duality gap**, and a
small gap is a certificate that a candidate is nearly optimal. **Strong duality**, a zero
gap at the optimum, holds for convex problems that satisfy Slater's condition. The dual
function is always concave, so the dual problem is convex even when the primal is not.

### The dual of a linear program, and shadow prices

For a linear program the dual is again a linear program. Take the workshop problem of
@sec-linear-programming, $\max\, 3x_1 + 5x_2$ subject to three machine-hour limits
$Ax \le b$ with $b = (4, 12, 18)$. Its dual is
$$
\min_{y \ge 0} \; 4y_1 + 12y_2 + 18y_3
\quad \text{s.t.} \quad
y_1 + 3y_3 \ge 3, \quad 2y_2 + 2y_3 \ge 5 .
$$
Read $y_i$ as the price of one hour on machine $i$. The constraints say that the hours
needed to make one unit of each product are worth at least the profit the product
earns, and the objective is the total value of all available hours. Strong duality says
that at the optimum, the total value of the hours equals the maximum profit.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-shadow-prices
#| tbl-cap: "The workshop problem's dual solution next to a direct experiment: add one hour to each machine and re-solve. The dual variables are exactly the marginal profit of each machine's hours. Machine 1 is not fully used at the optimum, so its price is zero (complementary slackness)."
from optimlab.optimizers.linear_programming import LinearProgram, dual, simplex

def workshop(hours):
    return LinearProgram(c=[-3.0, -5.0], A_ub=[[1, 0], [0, 2], [3, 2]], b_ub=hours)

hours = [4.0, 12.0, 18.0]
primal = simplex(workshop(hours))
prices = simplex(dual(workshop(hours))).x
rows = []
for i in range(3):
    more = list(hours)
    more[i] += 1
    gain = -simplex(workshop(more)).objective - (-primal.objective)
    rows.append((f"machine {i + 1}", f"{prices[i]:.2f}", f"{gain:.2f}"))
markdown_table(["constraint", "dual variable (shadow price)", "profit gained from +1 hour"], rows)
```

The maximum profit is `{python} f"{-primal.objective:.0f}"`, and so is the value of the
hours at their shadow prices, `{python} f"{np.dot(prices, hours):.0f}"`: zero duality
gap.

## The barrier method

The KKT conditions say what an optimum looks like. The barrier method is one way to
find it, for problems with inequality constraints: replace each hard wall with a smooth
penalty that becomes infinite at the wall, solve the resulting unconstrained problem with
Newton's method, and gradually make the penalty weaker relative to the objective.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition — Logarithmic barrier and central path"}
For $t > 0$, let
$$
x^\star(t) = \arg\min_x \; t\, f(x) - \sum_{i=1}^m \log\big(-g_i(x)\big).
$$
The curve $t \mapsto x^\star(t)$ is the **central path**. As $t \to \infty$ it converges
to a solution of the constrained problem.
:::

The logarithm is defined only where every $g_i(x) < 0$, so each barrier problem lives
strictly inside the feasible set and its minimizer stays away from the walls. Increasing
$t$ shifts the balance toward $f$, and the minimizer slides toward the boundary.

### Why the central path converges, and how fast

Setting the gradient of the barrier objective to zero gives
$$
t\, \nabla f(x) + \sum_i \frac{1}{-g_i(x)}\, \nabla g_i(x) = 0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\nabla f(x) + \sum_i \lambda_i \nabla g_i(x) = 0
\;\;\text{with}\;\; \lambda_i = \frac{1}{-t\, g_i(x)} > 0 .
$$
That is KKT stationarity, with positive multipliers. Complementary slackness does not
hold exactly: $\lambda_i\,(-g_i(x)) = 1/t$ instead of 0. The duality gap of this
primal–dual pair is therefore exactly $\sum_i \lambda_i\,(-g_i) = m/t$. Each point on the
central path certifies its own accuracy: it is within $m/t$ of optimal.

::: {.callout-note title="Algorithm — Barrier method"}
Given a strictly feasible $x$, an initial $t > 0$, a growth factor $\gamma > 1$ (typically
10 to 20) and a tolerance $\epsilon$:

1. **Centering**: starting from the current $x$, minimize $t f(x) - \sum_i \log(-g_i(x))$
   with Newton's method. The line search rejects any trial point that leaves the
   feasible set before testing for sufficient decrease.
2. **Stop** if $m/t < \epsilon$.
3. **Increase** $t \leftarrow \gamma t$ and go to step 1, warm-starting from the
   current point.
:::

The warm start is what makes this efficient: the previous center is close to the next
one, so each centering step needs only a few Newton iterations. The number of outer
iterations is about $\log\big(m/(t_0\epsilon)\big)/\log \gamma$ [@boyd2004convex, §11.3].
Interior-point methods for linear and convex programming refine this idea, and they
solve such problems in polynomial time.

A small example: minimize $(x_1 - 3)^2 + (x_2 - 3)^2$, a bowl centered at $(3, 3)$,
subject to $x_1 \le 1$ and $x_2 \le 1$. The constrained optimum is the corner $(1, 1)$,
where both constraints are active.

```{python}
#| label: barrier-setup
from optimlab.optimizers.barrier_method import ConstrainedProblem, barrier_method

problem = ConstrainedProblem(
    f=lambda x: (x[0] - 3.0) ** 2 + (x[1] - 3.0) ** 2,
    x0=np.array([0.5, 0.5]),
    inequality_constraints=[lambda x: x[0] - 1.0, lambda x: x[1] - 1.0],
    name="corner",
)
barrier = barrier_method(problem)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-central-path
#| fig-cap: "The central path for the corner problem. Each marker is the minimizer of one barrier problem; as t grows they move from the interior toward the corner (1, 1), reaching it only in the limit."
from optimlab.viz import central_path_figure

fig = central_path_figure(problem, barrier)
fig.update_layout(title="The central path")
fig.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-duality-gap
#| fig-cap: "The duality gap m/t after each outer iteration, on a log scale. Multiplying t by a fixed factor each round divides the gap by the same factor: a straight line, a geometric rate."
from optimlab.viz import duality_gap_figure

duality_gap_figure(barrier.grad_norm_trajectory, tol=1e-8).show()
```

The method reaches `{python} f"({barrier.x[0]:.6f}, {barrier.x[1]:.6f})"` in
`{python} barrier.n_iter` outer iterations. At that point the multipliers can be read off
the formula above, $\lambda_i = 1/(-t\, g_i(x))$, and stationarity can be checked
directly by drawing the vectors:

```{python}
#| label: fig-kkt-geometry
#| fig-cap: "KKT stationarity at the corner optimum: -∇f(x*) and the two active constraints' gradients, each scaled by its multiplier. The scaled constraint gradients add up (dashed) to exactly -∇f. The arrows are drawn with a small sideways offset only so that they do not overlap."
from optimlab.viz import kkt_geometry_figure

kkt_geometry_figure(problem, barrier).show()
```

Both multipliers are positive (both constraints are holding the optimum in place) and,
by the problem's symmetry, equal.

## ADMM: splitting a problem into easy pieces

The barrier method needs derivatives of everything. Many useful problems are sums of
pieces that are each easy to handle on their own but awkward together: a smooth data-fit
term plus a nonsmooth penalty, or terms that live on different machines. The
**alternating direction method of multipliers** [@boyd2011distributed] handles such sums
by giving each piece its own copy of the variable and using a multiplier to make the
copies agree.

### From the augmented Lagrangian to ADMM

Write $\min_x f(x) + h(x)$ as $\min_{x, z} f(x) + h(z)$ subject to $x = z$. The
**augmented Lagrangian** adds a quadratic penalty to the ordinary one:
$$
\mathcal{L}_\rho(x, z, \nu) = f(x) + h(z) + \nu^\top (x - z) + \frac{\rho}{2}\lVert x - z \rVert^2 .
$$
The classical *method of multipliers* minimizes $\mathcal{L}_\rho$ over $(x, z)$
jointly, then moves the multiplier uphill on the dual, $\nu \leftarrow \nu + \rho(x - z)$.
ADMM makes one change: instead of minimizing over $x$ and $z$ jointly, which is as hard
as the original problem, it minimizes over $x$ and then over $z$, once each. With the
scaled multiplier $u = \nu/\rho$, both minimizations become proximal steps
(@sec-least-squares):

::: {.callout-note title="Definition — ADMM (scaled form)"}
$$
\begin{aligned}
x_{k+1} &= \operatorname{prox}_{f/\rho}\big(z_k - u_k\big), \\
z_{k+1} &= \operatorname{prox}_{h/\rho}\big(x_{k+1} + u_k\big), \\
u_{k+1} &= u_k + x_{k+1} - z_{k+1} .
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

Each step touches only one piece of the objective, and neither needs to be
differentiable. For convex $f$ and $h$, ADMM converges for every $\rho > 0$. The
penalty $\rho$ is a speed setting, not a stability condition.

### Stopping: two residuals, not one

Two things must go to zero. The **primal residual** $\lVert x_k - z_k \rVert$ measures
whether the copies agree. The **dual residual** $\rho \lVert z_k - z_{k-1} \rVert$
measures whether $z$, and with it the multiplier, has stopped moving. It is tempting to
stop on the primal residual alone. That is unsafe: $x$ and $z$ can agree by coincidence
in the middle of a run, long before either is correct. On a lasso problem with
$\rho = 50$ it happens within a few iterations:

```{python}
#| label: admm-setup
import plotly.graph_objects as go

from optimlab.optimizers.admm import ADMMProblem, admm
from optimlab.optimizers.proximal_gradient import CompositeProblem, proximal_gradient, soft_threshold
from optimlab.viz.theme import contrasting_categorical, layout_template

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
m, n = 50, 20
A = rng.standard_normal((m, n))
x_true = np.zeros(n)
x_true[[2, 5, 9]] = [3.0, -2.0, 1.5]
b = A @ x_true + 0.01 * rng.standard_normal(m)
alpha = 1.0
AtA, Atb = A.T @ A, A.T @ b

def lasso_admm(rho):
    return ADMMProblem(
        prox_f=lambda v, t: np.linalg.solve(AtA + np.eye(n) / t, Atb + v / t),
        prox_g=lambda v, t: soft_threshold(v, alpha * t),
        x0=np.zeros(n),
        f_obj=lambda x: 0.5 * np.sum((A @ x - b) ** 2),
        g_obj=lambda x: alpha * np.sum(np.abs(x)),
    )

pg = proximal_gradient(
    CompositeProblem(grad_smooth=lambda x: A.T @ (A @ x - b),
                     prox_nonsmooth=lambda v, t: soft_threshold(v, alpha * t), x0=np.zeros(n)),
    lr=1.0 / np.linalg.eigvalsh(AtA).max(), max_iter=5000, tol=1e-10,
)
f_star = 0.5 * np.sum((A @ pg.x - b) ** 2) + alpha * np.sum(np.abs(pg.x))
run = admm(lasso_admm(50.0), rho=50.0, max_iter=5000, tol=1e-6, record_history=True)
primal = np.array(run.history["primal_residual"])
dual_res = np.array(run.history["dual_residual"])
first_dip = int(np.argmax(primal < 1e-6)) + 1
gap_at_dip = (run.f_trajectory[first_dip] - f_star) / f_star
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-admm-residuals
#| fig-cap: "ADMM on a lasso problem with ρ = 50 (log scale). The primal residual collapses to numerical zero early, a coincidence of x and z agreeing, while the dual residual and the objective's distance from the optimum are still large. The primal residual then rises again. Only when both residuals are small is the run actually finished."
colors = contrasting_categorical()
iters = np.arange(1, run.n_iter + 1)
fig = go.Figure([
    go.Scatter(x=iters, y=np.maximum(primal, 1e-17), name="primal residual ‖x − z‖",
               line={"color": colors[0], "width": 2}),
    go.Scatter(x=iters, y=np.maximum(dual_res, 1e-17), name="dual residual ρ‖zₖ − zₖ₋₁‖",
               line={"color": colors[1], "width": 2}),
    go.Scatter(x=iters, y=np.maximum(np.array(run.f_trajectory[1:]) - f_star, 1e-17),
               name="objective − optimum", line={"color": colors[2], "width": 2, "dash": "dot"}),
])
fig.update_layout(**layout_template(xaxis_title="iteration", yaxis_title="value",
                                    yaxis={"type": "log", "exponentformat": "power"},
                                    legend={"y": 1, "x": 1.02, "xanchor": "left"},
                                    margin={"r": 230}))
fig.show()
```

At iteration `{python} first_dip` the primal residual is below $10^{-6}$ while the
objective is still `{python} f"{100 * gap_at_dip:.0f}"`% above its optimal value. A
primal-only rule would have stopped there. The standard rule requires both residuals to
be small [@boyd2011distributed, §3.3.1], and the dual residual is far from small at that
point.

### ADMM and proximal gradient agree

The lasso was solved in @sec-least-squares by proximal gradient, which takes an explicit
gradient step. ADMM never takes one, yet the two land on the same answer:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-admm-rho
#| tbl-cap: "ADMM on the same lasso problem for several values of ρ. All converge to the proximal-gradient solution; ρ only changes how many iterations it takes."
rows = []
for rho in [0.5, 1.0, 5.0, 20.0, 50.0]:
    r = admm(lasso_admm(rho), rho=rho, max_iter=5000, tol=1e-6)
    rows.append((rho, r.n_iter, f"{r.f:.4f}", f"{np.max(np.abs(r.x - pg.x)):.1e}"))
markdown_table(["ρ", "iterations", "objective", "max difference from proximal gradient"], rows)
```

## When the unknown is a function: calculus of variations

So far the unknown has been a vector. In the calculus of variations it is a whole
function $y(x)$, and the objective is an integral, a *functional*:
$$
J[y] = \int_a^b F\big(x, y(x), y'(x)\big)\, dx, \qquad y(a), y(b) \text{ fixed}.
$$
The first-order condition is derived the same way as $\nabla f = 0$: perturb the
candidate and require the first-order change to vanish. Let $y + \epsilon\eta$ be a
perturbed curve, with $\eta(a) = \eta(b) = 0$ so the endpoints stay fixed. Then
$$
\frac{d}{d\epsilon} J[y + \epsilon \eta]\Big|_{\epsilon = 0}
= \int_a^b \big( F_y\, \eta + F_{y'}\, \eta' \big)\, dx
= \int_a^b \Big( F_y - \frac{d}{dx} F_{y'} \Big)\, \eta\, dx ,
$$
after integrating the second term by parts (the boundary term vanishes because $\eta$
does at both ends). For this to be zero for *every* perturbation $\eta$, the bracket
must vanish everywhere:

::: {.callout-note title="Definition — Euler–Lagrange equation"}
$$
\frac{\partial F}{\partial y} - \frac{d}{dx}\frac{\partial F}{\partial y'} = 0 .
$$
:::

It plays exactly the role of $\nabla f(x^\star) = 0$, now as a differential equation
[@gelfand2000calculus]. A classic instance is the soap film stretched between two
coaxial rings of radius $y_0$ a distance $\ell$ apart. The film minimizes its area,
$J[y] = 2\pi \int_0^\ell y \sqrt{1 + y'^2}\, dx$. Because $F$ does not depend on $x$
explicitly, the Euler–Lagrange equation has a first integral,
$F - y' F_{y'} = \text{const}$, which here reads $y / \sqrt{1 + y'^2} = c$, and its
solution is a **catenary**,
$$
y(x) = c \cosh\!\Big(\frac{x - \ell/2}{c}\Big), \qquad y_0 = c\cosh\!\Big(\frac{\ell}{2c}\Big).
$$

The same problem can be solved without any of this calculus. Represent $y$ by its values
on a grid of $N + 1$ points, replace the integral with a sum, and the functional becomes
an ordinary function of $N - 1$ unknowns (the interior heights), which BFGS
(@sec-gradient-methods) can minimize:

```{python}
#| label: fig-catenary
#| fig-cap: "Discretize, then optimize: starting from a flat film, BFGS on 39 interior heights bows the curve inward until it lies on the analytic catenary from the Euler–Lagrange equation."
import jax.numpy as jnp
from scipy.optimize import brentq

from optimlab.core import Problem
from optimlab.optimizers import bfgs

y0, ell, N = 1.0, 1.0, 40
xs = np.linspace(0.0, ell, N + 1)
dx = xs[1] - xs[0]

def area(y_inner):  # the 2π factor does not change the minimizer
    y = jnp.concatenate([jnp.array([y0]), y_inner, jnp.array([y0])])
    return jnp.sum((y[:-1] + y[1:]) / 2 * jnp.sqrt(1.0 + (jnp.diff(y) / dx) ** 2)) * dx

film = bfgs(Problem(f=area, x0=np.full(N - 1, y0)), max_iter=500)
y_opt = np.concatenate([[y0], film.x, [y0]])
c = brentq(lambda c: c * np.cosh(ell / (2 * c)) - y0, 0.5, 3.0)  # the stable (larger) root
y_catenary = c * np.cosh((xs - ell / 2) / c)
max_gap = np.max(np.abs(y_opt - y_catenary))

colors = contrasting_categorical()
fig = go.Figure([
    go.Scatter(x=xs, y=np.full(N + 1, y0), mode="lines", name="flat starting guess",
               line={"color": "#898781", "width": 1.5, "dash": "dot"}),
    go.Scatter(x=xs, y=y_catenary, mode="lines", name="catenary (Euler–Lagrange)",
               line={"color": "#52514e", "width": 4}),
    go.Scatter(x=xs, y=y_opt, mode="markers", name="BFGS on the discretized area",
               marker={"size": 6, "color": colors[0]}),
])
fig.update_layout(**layout_template(title="A soap film between two rings",
                                    xaxis_title="x", yaxis_title="radius y(x)"))
fig.show()
```

The largest gap between the optimized heights and the catenary is
`{python} f"{max_gap:.1e}"`. Solving the differential equation and minimizing a fine
discretization of the functional are, in the limit, the same computation. Direct
discretization is how most optimal-control problems are solved in practice, as
@sec-applications shows.

## What these examples cannot show

- **Scale.** Real interior-point solvers exploit sparsity in the Newton systems and
  handle equality constraints and infeasible starting points; the two-variable example
  shows the idea, not the engineering.
- **Non-convex constraints.** The KKT conditions remain necessary, but duality gaps can
  be positive, and a KKT point need not be a global optimum.
- **ADMM's speed.** ADMM reaches moderate accuracy quickly and high accuracy slowly. Its
  advantages, decomposition and parallelism, appear only on problems far larger than
  these.

## Connections

- **@sec-geometry**: the KKT conditions generalize $\nabla f(x^\star) = 0$, and
  convexity is what makes them sufficient.
- **@sec-linear-programming**: duality gives every linear program a twin, and its
  variables are the constraints' shadow prices.
- **@sec-least-squares**: proximal operators are ADMM's building blocks, and box
  constraints are the simplest constraints of all.
- **@sec-applications** applies the KKT system to portfolio selection, the barrier
  method to fair resource allocation, and discretize-then-optimize to optimal control.
